title: Family of dead victim agrees
article: Roman Andreichikov was jittery, jumpy and high on cocaine.
He was picking at his face, hopping around his Granville Street apartment and twice motioned as if to jump to his death from the balcony.
His friend, Rahim Hadini, couldn't handle the situation alone, so he called 911 for an ambulance.
Vancouver police were first at the scene.
"When they came in, they already had the Taser out," Hadini said of the May 1 encounter that claimed his friend's life.

Andreichikov was sitting on the couch by then and obeyed police orders to lie face down on the floor. There was a lot of yelling between the four officers and Andreichikov rolled over, as if to see what was going on, Hadini said.
"The cop with the Taser said, 'I'm going to shoot him,'" Hadini recalled.
Andreichikov was shot in the chest and as he was being held and handcuffed by the four officers, wheezed: "I can't breathe."
Within minutes, he was dead.
This week, Amnesty International called for a suspension of police use of Taser guns, citing two other B.C. fatalities and questioning the safety of the disabling device.
The human-rights watchdog alert is supported by Andreichikov's grieving mother, who believes Tasers are deadly and, at times, misused.
"He was having difficulties breathing but instead to give him help, they Tasered him down," says Diana Andreichikov.
Roman had no criminal record and was a healthy fitness instructor when he died, his mother says.
Vancouver police will say only that the Taser was used to subdue Andreichikov, who was suicidal after a long drug binge and that an investigation into his death is ongoing.
Tasers, which immobilize people with an electrical jolt, were designed as a non-lethal-force option for police.
But while Taser manufacturers insist the stun guns are safe, an Amnesty spokeswoman says the growing number of in-custody fatalities where Tasers were used are cause for concern.
"That particular type of police equipment has not been researched enough," says campaigner Hilary Homes.
In the U.S., where the use of Tasers is widespread, Amnesty has documented many cases of misuse and deaths related to heart attacks in cases where Tasers were used, Homes says.
Amnesty also questions two Canadian deaths that it highlighted this week in its 2004 human rights report -- Terry Hanna, in Burnaby, and Clayton Alvin Willey, in Prince George.
Both men were hit with Tasers during their arrests. Coroner's inquests in the two cases have yet to be held.
Hanna died at the scene. Willey's heart failed in hospital the day after his arrest, says his sister, Bryna Willey.
Willey has protested her brother's death by marching twice a week outside the Prince George RCMP detachment and has starting a petition to ban the use of Tasers.
Clayton was a heavy cocaine user and well known by local RCMP, she says. On the night he was arrested, he was high and trespassing into several yards.
The 911 report said Willey was carrying a knife, but what the caller actually saw was the glint of a silver cellphone, Bryna says.
According to witness reports, Clayton fought fiercely with police.
Bryna says her brother was badly beaten and, after the fight subsided, handcuffed and hogtied.
The Taser, she says, was a parting shot.
"He was shackled and on a gurney being put onto the ambulance when the Taser was used.
"That is a complete misuse of . . . an apprehension tool," she insists.
The RCMP say that a Taser was used to control Clayton during the struggle.
He died in hospital 16 hours later after suffering multiple heart attacks, Bryna says.
She is convinced the jolt from the Taser on her brother's already overtaxed system precipitated his heart failure.
If that proves true, no one will be more surprised than Steve Tuttle, spokesman for Taser International, the company that
supplies virtually all North American police departments with Taser guns.
Tasers have been widely used since 1999, he says, and "we have never been cited as a cause of death."
Tuttle says he is baffled by Amnesty's condemnation of a non- lethal means of control for police.
Tasers are not appropriate for use in every situation, but they do live up to their billing to "reduce injuries to suspects and officers."
Tuttle says many arrests involving Tasers are complicated by drug use.
In cases where suspects are in a state of excited delirium, their hearts race and they are prone to violent struggles and overexertion.
But it is the heart attack, not the Taser jolt, that kills, Tuttle says.
Homes is not convinced. In the same way that tear gas is lethal when sprayed in close quarters, Homes argues, it may be that Tasers are not appropriate in cases where people are high on drugs.
